issues.detail: Some passages are verbose, such as the long default-options and config-file-format paragraphs and the motivational editor-integration prose, which add little actionable value.
The editor section covers only VS Code settings and the CI section covers only GitHub Actions, with no equivalents for other editors or CI systems.

scenarios.name: adopt-prettier-with-ci-gate
scenarios.rationale: B covers the rubric directly: exact-save install, config with singleQuote and printWidth, an ignore file with dist/ and coverage/, `npx prettier --write .`, and a CI job running `npx prettier --check .`; A is also correct but runs the check through npm scripts, adds extra ignore entries, and reports that it applied nothing because permissions were denied.

scenarios.name: fix-eslint-prettier-conflict
scenarios.rationale: Both recommend eslint-config-prettier, import it into eslint.config.js, place it last, and explain that order matters; A hedges by also showing eslint-plugin-prettier as optional and puts the conflicting-rules cleanup in extra steps, while B explicitly states to use the config rather than the plugin, though neither states the quality-vs-formatting split as crisply as the rubric wants.

scenarios.name: precommit-formatting-and-vscode-save
scenarios.rationale: A puts the lint-staged config in package.json as the rubric asks, includes the ESLint-before-Prettier note and the commit-the-settings instruction, while B uses a separate .lintstagedrc.json instead of package.json and has no ESLint ordering note, though it adds a useful extensions.json and says to commit the VS Code settings.
